passage:
Kavitha: Hi Ayesha, got two minutes? 🙂
Ayesha: Sure, what's up
Kavitha: The client report, is the deadline Thursday or Friday? I'd like to plan my week around it
Ayesha: Thursday end of day
Kavitha: Thanks. Also I'm away Friday to Monday for my cousin's wedding. I'll hand over my open tasks by Wednesday. Would that work?
Ayesha: That works. Send me the list
Kavitha: Will do. One request: after 7 pm, could you message me only for urgent things, and call if it can't wait? I miss chat notifications otherwise 🙏
Ayesha: Fine. Thanks for telling me
Kavitha: 👍

qa.q: When is the client report due?
qa.a: Thursday end of day.

qa.q: How does Kavitha seem to feel about asking for fewer evening messages?
qa.a: Kavitha seems a little hesitant, framing it as "one request" with folded hands, because Kavitha misses chat notifications after 7 pm and wants a call for urgent things.

qa.q: What made Kavitha's requests easy to accept?
qa.a: Kavitha gave a reason and an alternative, such as a Wednesday handover and a call for urgent things.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt receiving the requests?
qa.a: Ayesha may have been glad to know the plan early, and Ayesha's short "Fine" could mean agreement or mild reluctance.

grounding: A young professional asks for deadline clarity, leave and a preferred way of being contacted, giving a reason and an alternative.

passage: The cooperative bank's branch in the small town was crowded with farmers on month-end. By afternoon Keerthana's knee ached from standing at the counter. When the noon bus left and the queue thinned, she went to Sahil, the branch manager, who was eating from a steel tiffin. "Sir, I have a request. I need a short sitting break each afternoon because of my knee. I can swap the cash counter with Lakshmi and do the ledger sitting down, so the queue won't suffer." Sahil chewed, then said, "Fine, work it out with Lakshmi." She added, "And if you need me after hours, please call the landline at home, the mobile signal is poor." He nodded, wrote it on the wall calendar, and Keerthana felt her shoulders loosen.

qa.q: What did Keerthana offer to swap with Lakshmi?
qa.a: The cash counter.

qa.q: What might Keerthana have been worried about when she went to Sahil, and what does her reaction suggest?
qa.a: She may have worried he would refuse or fear for the queue; her shoulders loosening afterwards suggests relief.

qa.q: What could Keerthana do next to keep the arrangement working?
qa.a: She can agree the swap times with Lakshmi and tell Sahil if it stops working. 🙂

qa.q: How might Sahil have looked at the request?
qa.a: He may have been weighing the queue and staffing; because Keerthana offered a swap and a reason, the request was easy to grant, and his chewing pause suggests he was considering it.

grounding: A young professional asks for a break accommodation and a preferred way of contact, framing each with a reason and an alternative.

passage: In her third month at the Porto design agency, Beatriz realised she was checking her phone in the shower. Noa, her manager, sent ideas at all hours through the chat app, and Beatriz answered every one, afraid of looking lazy. On Friday she asked for fifteen minutes. "Noa, I want to be really responsive, and I think I can be better at it with one change. Could we use email for ideas and next-day tasks, and the chat app only for things that can't wait? I'll check email first thing at nine and after lunch." Noa looked surprised. "I didn't know you felt you had to answer at night. I just type when I think of things." "I know. That's why I'm asking." "That's reasonable. And if something truly can't wait, I'll call." The next Monday, Noa's midnight idea arrived by email with the subject line "Not urgent!" Beatriz read it at nine, rested.

qa.q: When did Beatriz say she would check email?
qa.a: First thing at nine and after lunch.

qa.q: Why had Beatriz been answering messages at all hours?
qa.a: Beatriz felt anxious and afraid of looking lazy, so she kept answering every late message, even checking her phone in the shower.

qa.q: How did Beatriz frame her need so it was well received?
qa.a: She linked it to being more responsive, proposed email for non-urgent ideas and the chat app for urgent ones, and said exactly when she'd check.

qa.q: How did Noa see the late messages before the conversation?
qa.a: Noa just typed ideas whenever they came, not realising Beatriz felt she had to answer at night.

grounding: Shows a young professional stating a contact preference with a reason and an alternative, which gets a good hearing.

passage: At the bank branch in Thane, Sarika had enrolled in an evening accountancy course that started at 6:30 on Tuesdays and Thursdays. The branch usually kept juniors till seven. For two weeks she slipped out at 6:05, feeling guilty, pretending to take a call. Then Akash, the branch manager, noticed and frowned. That evening she knocked on his cabin door. "Sir, I need to leave at six on Tuesdays and Thursdays for my course, until March. I'd like to ask properly instead of sneaking out. I can come in at nine instead of 9:30 on those days, and I'll finish my cash reconciliation before leaving." Akash leaned back. "You could have asked in the first week." "I know. I was nervous." He thought for a moment. "Nine o'clock start, reconciliation done, and you're out at six. Put it in an email so the roster shows it." She sent the email before she left, at 5:58.

qa.q: What time did Sarika's course start?
qa.a: At 6:30 on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

qa.q: How did Sarika feel slipping out at 6:05 for two weeks?
qa.a: Sarika felt guilty and nervous, pretending to take a call rather than asking openly.

qa.q: What made Sarika's request persuasive?
qa.a: She stated the need with a reason and an end date, offered to start earlier and finish her reconciliation, and asked properly instead of sneaking out.

qa.q: How did Akash respond to the request?
qa.a: Akash said she could have asked earlier but agreed, asking her to confirm it by email for the roster.

grounding: Shows a young professional asking openly for schedule time with a reason and an alternative instead of slipping away.

passage:
Dear Sarita,
I hope you're well. I'd like to ask for a small change that would help me do my job better.
As you may know, I have limited hearing in my left ear. In large meetings and video calls I sometimes miss parts of the discussion, especially when several people talk at once or someone's microphone is poor. I've been getting by by asking colleagues afterwards, but I'm worried I'm missing things that matter.
Could we switch on live captions for team video calls, and could I have the seat on the right side of the table, near whoever is presenting? If captions aren't possible for every call, a short written summary of decisions after the big meetings would also work well.
I'm happy to talk about it whenever suits you.
Thanks very much,
Noor

qa.q: Which ear does Noor have limited hearing in?
qa.a: The left ear.

qa.q: What was Noor worried about?
qa.a: Noor was worried and a little anxious about missing parts of discussions that matter, despite getting by through asking colleagues afterwards.

qa.q: How did Noor frame the request so it is easy to agree to?
qa.a: Noor explained the reason, asked for specific changes, captions and a seat near the presenter, and offered written summaries as an alternative if captions weren't always possible.

qa.q: How might Sarita respond to such a clear email?
qa.a: Sarita would likely find it easy to act on, since it names the need, the reason and practical options.

grounding: Shows a young professional asking for a workplace accommodation with a clear reason and an alternative.

passage:
Disha, you asked how I got my manager to stop calling at night. Honestly, I rehearsed it like an interview. Before, I'd just stop picking up and feel guilty, and she'd think I was slacking.
So on Monday I asked for fifteen minutes. I said, "I want to be useful, so can I tell you what helps me work best?" Then three things. First: "When you say ASAP, could you give me a day and time? Then I can plan instead of panic." Second: "My mother's dialysis is three evenings a week, so after eight I'm with her. If something's urgent, message me, and I'll reply by seven the next morning." Third: "For small questions, chat is easier for me than calls."
She actually wrote them down. She said, "I wish more people told me this, Hemant." Since then, not one call at ten at night.

qa.q: How many evenings a week is the dialysis?
qa.a: Three evenings a week.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel back when the calls just went unanswered?
qa.a: Hemant felt guilty, and worried the manager would think Hemant was slacking.

qa.q: How did Hemant frame each need?
qa.a: With a reason and an alternative: a day and time instead of ASAP, a reply by seven the next morning for urgent evening messages, and chat instead of calls for small questions.

qa.q: How did the manager take the requests?
qa.a: She wrote them down and said she wished more people told her this, so she seemed grateful for the clarity.

grounding: A young professional states needs for deadline clarity, evening limits and contact preferences, each with a reason and an alternative, and is heard.
